_about: Changes that alter how agents behave. A new install starts with each one on. An install that already has agents gets each new entry switched off and waiting for its owner's decision: its lead agent reviews the change for that install and explains it, and the owner turns it on or leaves it off on the /changes page, or asks the lead in their own message to do it (behaviour_change, only for entries with leadMay true). leadMay is false for anything about security or spending limits: only the owner switches those, on the page. Add an entry here for any future change to agent behaviour; never switch one on for existing installs by itself. Optional field quiet: true marks a cheap, safe feature (no spending, no security, no behaviour risk): with leadMay true it arrives ON by itself on an existing install (by quiet-update) and shows once as a one-line notice on the card in the lead's chat until the owner acknowledges it; the owner can still turn it off. quiet with leadMay false counts as not quiet (it waits for the owner's decision like any other).

changes.title: Team advice in agents' instructions
changes.changes: Adds a short "running a team" section to agents' instructions: when to do a job themselves and when to hand it to a worker, which kind of model suits which job, how to write a brief, and how to get a second opinion and a critical check from a different model. Lead agents get the full version, other agents a core version, small local models and members' agents a short one. Turning it on gives it to the lead and to agents created from then on; agents that already exist get it only when it is switched on for them one by one (agent settings, Team guidance).
changes.benefits: Agents that hand out work do it more often and better: cheaper models for routine work, the strongest model kept for planning and hard reviews, important work checked by a second model before it is relied on.
changes.costs: About 450 words more in each lead turn's instructions (about 120 for the short version), and some extra worker or reviewer runs where an agent decides a job needs them.
changes.check: Which agents here already hand out work (consult_agent, spawn_workers) and how; whether their own instructions already cover delegation; which agents would benefit most (usually the primary agents that do long or many-part jobs).
changes.on: The lead and new agents get it; existing agents when switched on one by one.

changes.title: A starter team: a Challenger and three workers
changes.changes: Offers to create four agents: a Challenger that reviews important work adversarially, Scout for lookups and summaries, Builder for coding and multi-step work, Researcher for research and writing. They use cheaper models on the plans this install already pays for; the Challenger uses another company's model where one is connected. Turning it on shows a Set up your team card; nothing is created until the owner presses Create there. An agent name that is already taken is skipped.
changes.benefits: The lead has ready workers to hand routine work to and a second model to check important work, without setting them up by hand.
changes.costs: Each agent uses its model when it is given work; one billed per use is marked on the card before anything is created.
changes.check: Whether agents with these roles already exist here (a reviewer, a quick helper, a coder, a researcher), which models the workers would get, and whether any would be billed per use.
changes.on: The Set up your team card appears for an admin; agents are created only from it.
changes.off: No card and no starter agents.

changes.title: A spending limit: members' temporary helpers use only the models members may choose
changes.changes: This is a spending limit on family members' agents, not a change to your own agents. A member's agent can start temporary helpers for parts of a job. With this on, those helpers may run only on that agent's own model and the models the admin lets members choose for their own agents (the members' model list); any other model is refused. (The member limits on reasoning and speed apply to their helpers either way.) With it off, a member's temporary helpers may use any model this install reaches, as before.
changes.benefits: Members can't spend the owner's money on models the admin didn't allow them, for example a top model billed per use.
changes.costs: A member's agent that relied on a model outside the list for its workers gets a refusal naming the allowed models; the admin may need to add a model to the members' list.
changes.check: Whether this install has members, which models their agents use, what the members' model list holds, and whether members' agents start temporary helpers today. It limits spending; it does not change how the owner's own agents work.
changes.on: Members' temporary helpers are limited to the agent's own model and the members' model list.
changes.off: Members' temporary helpers may use any model this install reaches.

changes.title: The lead suggests new workers from how the install is used
changes.changes: Once a week the lead looks at a summary of how agents were used in the past seven days (requests per agent and model, errors, temporary workers it keeps starting) and, when a pattern would be better served by a permanent worker or specialist, proposes one to the owner in plain words: its name, job, model and what it would save or improve. At most one short proposal at a time; it builds one only on the owner's yes. For members' agents it uses counts only, never their conversations.
changes.benefits: Repeated work moves to the right agent and model over time instead of the lead redoing it, or a top model spending itself on routine jobs.
changes.costs: One short lead turn a week; occasionally a proposal to read.
changes.check: How busy this install is, whether the owner wants suggestions, and which agents do repeated work on expensive models.
changes.on: A weekly look and at most one proposal at a time (how often: weekly or off, set on this page).
changes.off: No weekly look and no proposals.

changes.title: Primary agents ask the lead for workers they need
changes.changes: Adds one line to primary agents' instructions: when they need a worker or a specialist they don't have, they ask the lead (by name) with the job, a proposed name and the model tier they think it needs; the lead decides with the owner. A member's main agent asks through its existing request to an admin instead, and a member's other agents ask that member's main agent; they never reach the admin's agents.
changes.benefits: Gaps in the team surface to the lead and the owner instead of an agent struggling on its own.
changes.costs: Now and then a request for the lead to answer.
changes.check: Which primary agents exist here and whether the lead should hear from them.

changes.title: Primary agents keep long work on track with check-ins
changes.changes: When a primary agent starts or hands off work that will outlast its reply (a project another agent leads, a background job, a batch of workers, anything expected to take more than about 15 minutes), it schedules its own check-in: every 30 minutes by default, sooner for short jobs, less often for overnight work, and only one per piece of work. Each check-in reads the status cheaply, unblocks or answers what is waiting, tells you only about a decision you must make, a blocker or the finished work, and cancels itself when the work is done. Work that shows no progress across two check-ins is reported to you in plain words. The lead gets the full instructions, other primary agents a short version.
changes.benefits: Long work doesn't quietly stall: someone looks at it on a schedule, unblocks it, and you hear about it when it matters, not all the time.
changes.costs: A short turn of the agent's model at each check-in while work is running (with the default, two an hour per piece of work), and about 150 words more in the lead's instructions (about 70 for other primary agents). Members' main agents get it too, on the models you allow them.
changes.check: Whether agents here start long work (projects led by other agents, background jobs, batches of workers), whether they already schedule their own follow-ups, and whether the owner wants fewer or more updates.
changes.on: Primary agents schedule and run check-ins on their long work.
changes.off: Agents follow up only when they decide to on their own.

changes.title: Primary agents suggest better ways of working
changes.changes: When a primary agent sees a better way to get your kind of work done, it says so in one or two lines and asks: a specialist for a subject that keeps coming back, a dedicated lead agent for a long project so your main agent stays free, a batch of low-cost helpers for work that can run in parallel, a cheaper model or speed for routine jobs, a scheduled task instead of a manual repeat, a Record for facts it keeps asking for again, or anything else that would make things easier for you. At most one suggestion per topic and only when it is relevant; after a no it remembers and does not suggest it again; nothing is created without your yes, and new agents are built by the lead (a member's agent asks through its request to an admin).
changes.benefits: Your agents get better at your work over time and point out savings you might not know about, without you having to know what is possible.
changes.costs: About 170 words more in each primary agent's instructions; now and then a one- or two-line suggestion to answer (at most one per conversation); a yes may add an agent or a scheduled task. Members' main agents get it too; theirs ask an admin through their request.
changes.check: How the owner uses the primary agents today, whether there are repeated jobs or long projects that a specialist, a project lead or cheaper models would serve better, and whether the owner welcomes suggestions.
changes.on: Primary agents make short suggestions when they are relevant.
changes.off: No suggestions about better ways of working.

changes.title: Primary agents hand long work to a build partner and stay free to talk
changes.changes: A primary agent no longer waits on long work inside its own turn. Anything longer than a few minutes (development, production, long research) goes to its build partner or another teammate with hand_off, and the agent is free to talk with you at once. The other agent keeps a status file next to the brief, and its report comes back to your agent when it is done. When the lead creates a primary agent for long development or creative work, it also creates that agent's build partner.
changes.benefits: You can talk to your main agents while long work is running, ask how it is going and change course, instead of waiting until the work ends.
changes.costs: About 150 words more in each primary agent's instructions (a few more for the lead). A build partner is one more agent, on a model the lead chooses from what you already have (subscription before pay-per-use). Each hand-off costs the other agent's turns, as the same work would cost on workers.
changes.check: Which primary agents here run long work (development, production, long research) and wait on workers or consultations inside their own turns, whether they already have a build partner or a teammate that can take it, and which model a partner would use.
changes.on: Primary agents get the rule and hand long work off; the lead creates a build partner with each new primary agent for long development or creative work.
changes.off: Primary agents may still wait on long work inside their own turns, as before; hand_off stays available when they choose it.

changes.title: Primary agents split complex work across parallel workers, never at the cost of quality
changes.changes: For any complex task, a primary agent first splits the work into independent parts and runs them at the same time without being asked: several workers or consultations at once, several leads or hand-offs, reviews from different companies' models side by side. It picks a model for each part from the models it may use: a cheaper one for volume where it does that part as well, the strongest where the part decides the quality; an agent whose work must stay on its own service (a medical or legal team agent, for example) keeps every worker and reviewer on its own model and works only with agents on its own service. Quality comes first: work stays in one thread where splitting would make it worse (one design or writing voice, tightly coupled changes to the same files, a chain of decisions that build on each other, the final judgement and putting the parts together), and the agent says in one line why. It checks every part that comes back and puts the parts together itself, and never splits trivial jobs or quick look-ups. Work that will take more than a few minutes still goes to a teammate with hand_off, and the agent leading it does the splitting. When the lead's other leads are all busy and work is waiting, the lead may create another lead rather than lend a specialist from another field.
changes.benefits: Complex jobs finish sooner without you having to ask for parallel work, the agent checks each part before using it, and work that is better done by one hand stays with one.
changes.costs: About 220 words more in each primary agent's instructions (about 260 for the lead). Complex jobs start several worker, consultation or review runs at once, each on the model the agent picks for its part, so a job uses more of a plan's allowance or pay-per-use budget at the same time, with some extra runs where a part is checked twice. A new lead is one more agent, on a model from what you already have. Members' main agents get it too, within the limits you set for members.
changes.check: Which primary agents here take on complex, many-part jobs and whether they already run parts in parallel or only when asked, which cheaper models they could use for volume, whether pay-per-use models would be picked for parallel parts, and whether the leads are often busy with work waiting.
changes.on: Primary agents split complex work into parallel parts by themselves, keep in one thread what splitting would hurt and say why, and check every part.
changes.off: Agents run work in parallel only when they decide to or are asked, as before.

changes.title: Protect your Maestro's own code
changes.changes: Agents can no longer change the program files of your Maestro on this computer: everything in its folder except your data, the agents' workspaces and installed packages. That includes git commands that change those files (stash pop, checkout, reset, pull and the like). An agent that is refused is told to describe the change to you instead. This applies to every agent, the lead too.
changes.benefits: A change an agent makes to your Maestro's code can stop the next update or break your Maestro so that every agent turn fails. With this on, that cannot happen by an agent's hand; you decide what changes, and the lead describes what it would like to change.
changes.costs: An agent that maintains your Maestro's code, as on a developer's install, cannot do its work while this is on. The check reads a file of yours (data/behaviour-reviews.json); if it cannot be read, the protection stays on and Setup shows a notice.
changes.check: Ask your lead to add a line to a file in lib/: it is refused with the message that your Maestro's own code is protected. Whether any agent here maintains your Maestro's code (a developer's install), in which case you may want this off.
changes.on: No agent can change your Maestro's program files on this computer, or run git commands that change them.
changes.off: Agents with the right to write there can change the code. Needed only if an agent maintains your Maestro's code, as a developer's install does.

changes.title: Your lead leaves your Maestro's code alone
changes.changes: Adds a short section to your lead's instructions: it never changes your Maestro's own program files on this computer, describes the change to you instead and offers to send it to the project as an idea or a pull request, warns you plainly if you insist on a local change (it stops updates), and never puts back changes that were put aside (git stash pop or apply).
changes.benefits: Your lead explains what it would change instead of editing code that your updates replace, so updates keep working.
changes.costs: About 120 words more in the lead's instructions in every turn.
changes.check: Whether your lead has been editing your Maestro's files on this computer, and whether anything here depends on such a local change.
changes.on: The lead gets the rule and leaves your Maestro's code alone.
changes.off: The lead gets no such rule; "Protect your Maestro's own code" can still refuse the edits.

changes.title: Agents offer deep research when a question needs it
changes.changes: Gives agents a deep research tool and a short section in their instructions. When a question needs real research (the current state of a field, comparisons, what is best, recent findings), the agent offers a deep research run and the person answers Yes, No, Always yes or Never; Always yes and Never are remembered for that person and can be changed in Settings. A yes runs in the background: helpers on a fast, inexpensive model research parts of the question and read the actual sources, then the agent's own model checks and summarises them; the report, with a verdict first, links, dates and how confident it is, arrives in the same chat. A person who chose Never is reminded now and then (once a week by default) that it is off.
changes.benefits: Much better answers to research questions: many searches and the sources themselves instead of one or two searches, with the evidence and disagreements laid out. The person stays in charge of when it runs, and can keep talking while it does.
changes.costs: About 80 words more in agents' instructions in every turn. Each run uses several helper runs and one summary run: several times a normal answer, from the plan's allowance on a subscription or paid per use on an API key. Nothing runs without a yes, or an Always yes the person chose.
changes.check: Which agents here answer research questions, which models their helpers may use (a member's agents only the models an admin allows), whether web search works on this install, and how much pay-per-use budget a run could take.
changes.on: Agents offer deep research on research questions; each person decides each time or once for all.
changes.off: No agent offers deep research; agents answer research questions as before.

changes.title: Agents may start quick research for their own work, and a question nobody answers starts a quick run
changes.changes: Works together with "Agents offer deep research when a question needs it" and does nothing while that one is off. (1) An agent that needs research for work it is doing itself, not for a question you asked, can start a quick run without asking you. It must give a one-sentence reason, it never waits for you, and it can only start the quick level: a thorough run starts only when you choose it. (2) When an agent asks you whether to research a question and you do not answer within the wait (two minutes by default; you can change it in Settings, 0 means no question is shown and a quick run starts at once), a quick run starts and the report says so on its first line. (3) When an agent asks in a turn you did not start, such as a scheduled task, it is handled like the agent's own work. Each such run shows a notice in that agent's chat and on your phone, with the question, the reason and the cost, and two buttons: Stop, and Make it thorough. The report goes to the agent, and to you only when you chose Make it thorough or when nobody answered your question. There is a daily limit on runs started this way: 3 per agent and 10 for the whole install by default, changeable in Settings (0 means no limit). A person who chose Never is never overridden, and the wait you set also applies to the question card while this change is off.
changes.benefits: Agents doing a long task can look things up properly instead of guessing or stopping to ask, and a question you missed while away still gets researched. You keep the last word: you can stop any run, or make it thorough, and the daily limit keeps it from running away.
changes.costs: Runs started without your yes use your plan allowance or pay-per-use budget like any quick run: several times a normal answer each, up to the daily limit (by default 10 a day across the install, 3 per agent).
changes.check: Which agents here run long tasks or scheduled work that would use research, what a quick run costs on their models (plan allowance or pay-per-use), whether the daily limits of 3 per agent and 10 for the install suit this install, and whether two minutes is a fair wait before a question starts a run by itself.
changes.on: Agents may start quick research for their own work within the daily limits, and an unanswered question starts a quick run after the wait.
changes.off: Agents cannot start research for their own work; an unanswered question gets a normal answer with a one-line offer at the end, as before.
